transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-02
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Aisha (Nimbus CTO), Ben (Platform), Sofia (ML)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll run through autoscaling and capacity planning for your inference workloads. quick agenda: reserved capacity, burst pools, queueing/backpressure, cache warmers, batching/quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem notes.
[00:18] Aisha: Sounds good, we're mainly worried about spikes from our portal—telemetry shows big bursts when doctors sync notes at shift changes. 99th pct latency budget is 350ms for text-gen endpoints.
[00:35] Diego: ok, so two constraints: tight p99 latency, and bursty traffic. that pushes us toward reserved GPUs for base load plus a burst pool for spikes. do you have average rps and peak rps numbers?
[00:50] Ben: average is ~45 rps, peak up to 420 for 20-45s when a sync job runs. payloads are about 600-1200 tokens per request.
[01:10] Diego: that token range matters for batching and KV cache size. if you use prefix caching for frequent prompts, you'll often avoid full context recompute but cache warmup matters.
[01:30] Sofia: quick q — how much does the KV cache affect required GPU memory? we saw eviction issues during long sessions.
[01:40] Diego: KV cache is per-session and scales with sequence length * num_layers * head_dim; in our benchmarks a 1.5k token worst case pushes cache to ~8-10GB for our 7B model variant. that means you should plan for instance types with extra memory headroom, or choose quantized variants that shave memory.
[02:05] Maya: high level rec: reserved capacity sized to handle sustained baseline plus a small safety margin, and a burst pool (shared, lower-priority) to absorb short spikes. the trick is sizing the reserved pool so you don't overpay but still meet your p99 SLO.
[02:25] Aisha: ok, show the queue model you recommend. our infra team prefers queuing over shedding.
[02:34] Diego: we've got two patterns: 1) Soft queueing with rate-limit thresholds and time-based backpressure — short queue slots (50–200ms) and then spill to burst; 2) Hard shedding for extremely long or non-critical batch jobs. for your p99 350ms we recommend soft queueing with per-request latency budget of 250ms on reserved nodes then fallback to burst with an added tail latency allowance.
[03:10] Ben: can you walk through a numeric example?
[03:15] Diego: sure. baseline 45 rps, assume average token cost ~0.02s per token on a reserved GPU with batching disabled for low latency, so 600 tokens => ~12s (note: rough numbers), but we normally use partial streaming and dynamic batching to keep tail low. for planning we convert token processing to effective qps equivalent — simpler: measure throughput of the model on your chosen instance. if one reserved GPU handles ~30 concurrent low-latency sessions, you'd need 2 GPUs for baseline. then configure burst pool to add another 6 GPUs for spikes.
[03:55] Sofia: those per-token times seem high? there's some noise in transcribed numbers — perhaps Diego meant ms per token.
[04:02] Diego: right — sorry, ms. 0.02s = 20ms per token, so 600 tokens ≈ 12,000ms naive, but streaming/prefix reuse reduces end-to-end to within target. the important bit is measuring effective end-to-end latency with your prompt templates.
[04:25] Maya: yes, we always recommend customers run bench with their exact prompt set and sequence length distribution. Diego, will share our benchmark template.
[04:34] Aisha: on bursting — do you offer pre-warmed instances? we worry about cold-starts adding 300–900ms.
[04:43] Diego: we support pre-warm and instant-burst policies. pre-warm keeps a minimum number of nodes in warm state — faster startup, higher cost. instant-burst taps into pooled capacity which may add ~200–400ms depending on queue/backfill. you can set a hybrid: keep 1-2 pre-warmed nodes per region + burst pool for big spikes.
[05:12] Ben: how do you account for batching? we need low latency, so we generally avoid large batches.
[05:18] Diego: Redwood runtime supports dynamic batching: it will batch small windows (like 2–6 requests) when it doesn't break latency SLOs. you can set max_await_time and max_batch_size. for p99 350ms, set max_await_time to 15ms and max_batch_size to 8 initial guess, then tune from load tests. batching can reduce GPU cost by 20–40% but increases tail.
[05:48] Sofia: quantization — we want to use 4-bit to save memory. any gotchas?
[05:53] Diego: quantization can reduce mem and improve throughput, but watch for quality regressions on certain prompts. our recommendation: use quantized model variants in burst pool where slight degradation is acceptable, keep full-precision in reserved pool. and run A/B evals on held prompt sets.
[06:15] Aisha: for VPC/on-prem, how different is the autoscale story? we'd prefer private with our own infra.
[06:23] Diego: on-prem you have full control but you lose Redwood's global burst pool. autoscaling there depends on your cluster scheduler — we provide a private control plane and autoscaler hooks. recommended pattern: reserve base capacity in your cluster, keep a small hot pool, and configure node/GPUs with fast provisioning firmware; also integrate our cache warmers to reduce latency after failover.
[06:48] Ben: any recommendations for instance types? we're on G4dn-like equivalents.
[06:53] Diego: for your workload 80–100 token sequences, a single A10G-equivalent handles more concurrency; if you have long sequences (1k+ tokens) prefer higher memory instances like A100 or H100. quantization reduces memory pressure so can enable smaller instances.
[07:12] Maya: let's talk metrics — what to track in prod to validate autoscale policies?
[07:17] Diego: track: request rate (rps), queue length, node utilization (GPU% and memory%), KV cache hit ratio, cold-start counts, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), model switch frequency (if fallback occurs), and cost per token. alarms on sustained GPU util >80% and p99 > target.
[07:45] Sofia: KV cache hit ratio — how high do we need it to be to justify pre-warm?
[07:50] Diego: depends, but >60% hit ratio materially reduces compute. pre-warming helps maintain cache locality for long-lived sessions, which is good for interactive workflows.
[08:05] Aisha: about pricing — if we reserve 2 GPUs and allow bursts of 6 GPUs, how does billing look?
[08:12] Maya: reserved GPUs are committed capacity monthly; burst is usage-based. we'll send you a simple pricing sheet. generally cost = reserved monthly fee + usage * burst_rate + request-level units; burst is billed by GPU-hour and token usage.
[08:38] Ben: what about queueing thresholds — we want to avoid queueing beyond 200ms. can we have Redwood automatically spill to burst when queue > 100ms?
[08:48] Diego: yes you can set policy: if avg queued_time > 100ms for 30s, autoscale-up by N GPUs or route new requests to burst. have a cooldown window to avoid oscillation.
[09:05] Aisha: oscillation is a real concern — we use Kubernetes HPA but had thrashing on other services. any recommended smoothing?
[09:13] Diego: add a scaling hysteresis: require metric sustained for T seconds, use step-up/step-down rules, and prefer gradual ramping when possible. also use predictive scaling based on time-of-day or known cron syncs; for your doctor shift spikes, schedule anticipatory scale-up 30s before expected events.
[09:36] Sofia: can Redwood's control plane run predictive rules?
[09:39] Diego: yes, we support scheduled and predictive policies; predictive rules can be fed by your traffic histogram. we can ingest simple cron-like schedules or a more advanced ML predictor if desired.
[09:55] Maya: let's talk about a pilot layout recommendation for Nimbus. high level: 1) baseline reserved pool: 2 gpus to cover sustained 45 rps, 2) surge/burst pool: up to 6 additional gpus on demand, 3) pre-warm 1 node per region, 4) dynamic batching limits: await 15ms, size 8, 5) quantized variants in burst only, 6) KV cache warming on deployment and session affinity for interactive flows.
[10:35] Ben: that seems reasonable. what's the expected tail latency for that setup?
[10:40] Diego: if tuned, p99 should be within your 350ms budget most of the time; big spikes beyond burst capacity will add queueing or degrade p99. hence the pilot to tune thresholds.
[10:55] Aisha: ok, on the security/VPC front — we need SOC2 and KMS integration plus audit logs.
[11:02] Maya: Redwood supports KMS/HSM integrations, SOC2-compliant ops for hosted, and Private deployment with customer-managed KMS. we'll schedule a security deep-dive next week.
[11:15] Sofia: one more on metrics — can we get token-level cost breakdown?
[11:20] Maya: yes our console has token-level cost and per-route breakdowns. we'll share screenshots in the follow-up.
[11:30] (short technical aside)
[11:34] Diego: one practical tip: use session pinning for chat-like flows so KV cache stays hot and you avoid repeated cache rebuilds that spike memory and startup time.
[11:50] Ben: for live experiments, how do we do canaries?
[11:53] Diego: we support canary rollouts by traffic percentage and model variant. start with 5% traffic on new autoscale rules and monitor p99 and error rates for 24–48 hours, then increase. automated rollback if p99 regresses beyond threshold.
[12:10] Aisha: are there logs we should collect for postmortems?
[12:13] Diego: collect: request traces, model switch events, queue/backpressure metrics, node provisioning times, and KV cache eviction events. we also emit deployment trace ids that you can correlate with your app logs.
[12:30] Maya: okay let's recap next steps and owners.
[12:34] Maya: Diego will share benchmark worksheet and recommended autoscale policy; Maya will send pricing and reserved/burst options; Aisha will share traffic histograms and finalize SLOs; we'll set security/VPC deep-dive with Nimbus infra team.
[12:55] Aisha: thanks, can we get the benchmark template today?
[12:58] Diego: yes, I'll upload it right after this call.
[13:05] (end of recording)
